Patrick Flynn's birthplace is in dispute: Ireland, as given in both the 1850 and 1860 U.S. censuses, vs. Pennsylvania, as given in the 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate. The birthplace matters because it bears on Patrick's immigration history and on the reliability of the sources used to establish his parentage.

The 1850 census (a_002, src_001) records Patrick's birthplace as Ireland. The informant was almost certainly Thomas Flynn or his wife — the head of household and his spouse, both Irish-born themselves, reporting to the enumerator about a child living in their home when Patrick was approximately five years old. The 1860 census (a_009, src_003) independently records the same birthplace, from the same household, a decade later. Because both censuses derive from the same family informant class, they carry the weight of one well-situated informant confirmed across two enumerations. The 1908 death certificate (a_012, src_004) records Patrick's birthplace as Pennsylvania. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. Brown was not present at Patrick's birth, had no firsthand knowledge of where Patrick was born, and is reporting a fact that would have reached him only through family conversation — if at all.

The census evidence is more reliable. Thomas Flynn and his wife were the persons closest to the fact of Patrick's birth; they would have known where their child was born. Two recordings a decade apart are consistent. James Brown's Pennsylvania entry, by contrast, comes from a man with no epistemic access to this fact.

Brown's error follows the immigration-origin confusion pattern documented in Irish-American families: Patrick emigrated as a small child and spent his entire adult life in Pennsylvania. Brown knew Patrick only as a Pennsylvanian. When asked for a birthplace on the death certificate, Brown almost certainly reported what he associated with Patrick — Pennsylvania, the state where Patrick lived — rather than Ireland, a country Brown may never have heard Patrick mention as his birthplace. This is a well-attested pattern: American-resident relatives of immigrants commonly report the state of American settlement rather than the country or place of actual birth, especially when the immigrant arrived in early childhood and the foreign birth had little relevance to family identity by the next generation. Ireland is accepted as Patrick's birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant incompetence for this specific fact.
